{#cgsy} # Discussion

{#o8pf} In our population-based cohort study we found that BCa patients with diabetic glucose level had worse survival compared to normoglycemic ones as hypothesized, regardless of whether diabetic hyperglycemia occurred before or after BCa. Expectedly, also overall mortality was higher in diabetics compared to non-diabetics.

{#yd2w} # Hyperglycemia and bladder cancer prognosis in a Finnish population-based cohort

{#ngxc} # Abstract

{#crw4} **Background: **Diabetes might increase risk of bladder cancer (BCa) incidence and bladder cancer specific death.

{#mvjk} **Objective: **To assess the potential association between diabetes and prognosis of BCa.

{#m3fd} **Design, setting and participants: **Register-based cohort study included 14,638 participants with BCa diagnosed in Finland during 1995–2012. Three databases were used to obtain information on BCa, diabetes and comorbidities. Hyperglycemia was determined by blood glucose or HbA1c. The role of antidiabetic medication use was also assessed.

{#mh15} **Outcome measurements and statistical analysis: **Associations between diabetes and BCa-specific and overall mortality were evaluated using multivariable Cox regression models.

{#zjp1} **Results and limitation: **During median follow-up of 4.3 years after BCa diagnosis 3,582 (24.5%) participants died of BCa. Diabetic post-diagnostic blood glucose level was associated with worse BCa-specific HR 1.58 (1.10–2.28) and overall survival HR 1.50 (1.20–1.89). The risk increase was slightly lower among hyperglycemic DM medication users (HR 1.43 (0,68–3.02) than non-users HR 1.80 (1.13–2.85). The main limitation of this study was insufficient information on tobacco smoking.

ops.markdown: Anti-DM medication users underwent cystectomy less often than non-users, whereas the frequency of cystectomy did not differ by glycemic status. This pattern is in line with the literature: a meta-analysis of 5 cohort studies showed that diabetes is significantly associated with poor overall and cancer-specific survival after radical cystectomy in bladder cancer patients [@w:w15]. The same study further suggested that diabetes is a risk factor for life-threatening complications in cystectomy patients after surgery and is positively associated with serious complications. Because diabetics often have comorbidities affecting their suitability for surgical treatment, they might be treated in a less aggressive manner [@w:w16]. Nevertheless, around 24% of participants with diabetic glycemic status underwent this operation. Uncontrolled diabetes has also been linked to increased risk of postoperative complications after cystectomy [@w:w17], and Oh et al. found elevated risk of BCa recurrence, cancer-specific and overall mortality among diabetics in a cohort of BCa patients who underwent cystectomy [@w:w18]. Importantly, our analysis showed an increased risk of BCa death by diabetes after adjustment for primary BCa treatment, indicating that the observed survival association is not explained by differing treatment alone. In the meta-analysis by Dong et al., which pooled 5 cohort studies of bladder cancer patients treated with radical cystectomy (2,661 patients, 391 with diabetes), diabetes was associated with higher overall mortality (HR 1.36, 95% CI 1.30–1.43, P<0.001) and cancer-specific mortality (HR 1.59, 95% CI 1.29–1.95, P<0.001) [@c:c25d3cd3]; the latter estimate is comparable to the HR 1.58 (95% CI 1.10–2.28) for BCa death observed in our cohort, suggesting that the excess risk persists even in a uniformly cystectomised population.
